name: TSMP
listed_description: An intrusion and macro-free C++20 library for static reflection. It uses libclang to extract reflection data from your source code and makes it usable via template specialization.
reason: No benchmark, number or baseline anywhere reachable. Readme.md (257 lines) has no performance section; repo tree (doc has only Changelog.md, test, examples, tooling) has no benchmark directory. Readme says the library is not production ready. A web search for reflection-library comparisons found none that include it.

name: visit_struct
listed_description: A miniature library for struct-field reflection in C++.
reason: Directional claim only. README says visitation resolves at compile time with no run-time overhead and no performance hit versus run-time polymorphism, but gives no numbers and no benchmark against Boost.Fusion, Boost.Hana or Boost.PFR (it only compares API ergonomics and compiler support). No benchmark directory in the repo; a web search for a third-party compile-time or run-time shootout including it found none.

name: WJElement
listed_description: Advanced JSON manipulation library, with support for JSON Schema.
reason: Directional claim only. README says WJReader and WJWriter are optimized for speed and memory-efficiency, with no numbers and no named baseline. Repo has docs, examples, include, src and Windows files but no benchmark. A web search for a JSON-parser shootout including it found none.

name: Xalan C
listed_description: A library and a command line program to transform XML documents using a stylesheet that conforms to XSLT 1.0 standards.
reason: No performance numbers in the repo (docs/ has build, faq, overview, samples and similar pages, nothing on benchmarks). Only third-party evidence found is old mailing-list material (GNOME xslt list, 2001-2003) that could not be opened because lists.gnome.org, sourceware.org, dspace.cuni.cz and groups.google.com are egress-blocked. Search snippets say libxslt was about 15 percent faster than Xalan-C on average, with one exception: recursive Fibonacci fib(27) at 17.6 s on xalan-c versus 21.7 s on xsltproc 1.0.3 (attributed in a search summary to a 2001-October thread, https://lists.gnome.org/archives/xslt/2001-October/msg00092.html; unverified here, no hardware or flags known). Possible lead for a session that can reach that list: single cherry-picked win, tier C at best.

name: Xerces-C++
listed_description: A validating XML parser written in a portable subset of C++.
reason: No performance claim in the repo mirror https://github.com/apache/xerces-c (doc/ has guides, FAQs, samples; no benchmark pages). xerces.apache.org, pugixml.org and codesynthesis.com are egress-blocked. Search snippets show third-party benchmarks (pugixml benchmark, 2006 libxml2 mailing-list posts, tibleiz asm-xml) place Xerces-C++ behind Expat, libxml2 and pugixml, so it is the slow baseline there. Possible lead only: CodeSynthesis XSDBench (2006, https://codesynthesis.com/projects/xsdbench/) compares schema-validation throughput of Xerces-C++ with libxml2, MSXML and Oracle XDK; results not reachable, so whether Xerces-C++ wins any row is unknown.

name: yaml-cpp
listed_description: A YAML parser and emitter in C++.
reason: No performance claim in README or repo. Only benchmarks found put it last: rapidyaml README (https://github.com/biojppm/rapidyaml) shows yaml-cpp at 22.53 MB/s parse and 6.27 MB/s emit, slower than libyaml 135.06, libfyaml 149.15, jsoncpp 298.60 and nlohmann 197.17 MB/s parse, and says ryml is generally 30x (parse) and 150x (emit) faster. No row where yaml-cpp beats a named baseline.
